newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Bruton asks Ireland to stick with his coalition.
newsitem.headline: Bruton asks Ireland to stick with his coalition.

text.p: Decent. Determined. Dull. Prime Minister John Bruton went into the final television debate of Ireland's election campaign on Wednesday night knowing that even his friends described him in this way.
For almost an hour he held off the pugnacious challenge of his main rival, Bertie Ahern, with what the Irish Times called on Thursday "the best performance of his political life".

Calm, measured and assured, Bruton answered the critics who say he has neither passion nor charisma and appealed to voters to stick with the government that has overseen Ireland's economic boom for the past two and a half years.

The leader of an unlikely coalition with the radical Democratic Left and Labour party, Bruton voiced confidence that history would be forgotten and Ireland's voters would return a government for the first time in three decades.
He let Ahern spout a confusing ream of figures showing that Bruton's so-called Rainbow coalition has allowed government spending to increase by eight percent against a targetted four.
"I make no apology for spending that money. Justice does not come cheap. I have no apology to make to any economist for spending money to improve education," Bruton said.

Once dubbed the most unpopular finance minister in Irish history for introducing a tax on children's shoes, Bruton admitted: "I have made a lot of mistakes in my political career, but I have learned from them."

It was a performance of dignity, critics said, and may yet prove a defining moment in a campaign in which Bruton's Fine Gael and coalition allies have trailed consistently behind the opposition Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrats.

It was not always so. Bruton's political career seemed in limbo until the end of 1994, when he put together a coalition after the previous alliance of Fianna Fail and Labour collapsed in a row over legal appointments.

The alliance turned what looked like the twilight of his political career into a new dawn, which included steering the EU's rotating presidency in 1996 and a historic visit by U.S. President Bill Clinton in the previous year.
"I am a Christian Democrat. All over Europe Christian Democrats are in coalition with other parties. Our partnership is one that works and will continue to work," he says.

"He may seem ponderous, but he weighs his words. He knows what he wants," said a political contemporary. "He scented the collapse of the government (in 1994) for months and knew his day would come one way or the other."

Bruton, 50, is the only prominent Fine Gael personality with any lengthy government experience. A junior minister in the 1970s while he was in his 20s, he served as a full cabinet member in the 1980s, the last time Ireland had a minority government.

After the tax-on-shoes budget,which brought down the government, he survived when Fine Gael went back into opposition and won the leadership of the party in 1990 after a wounding battle with Alan Dukes.

His policy on Northern Ireland has been characterised by a concern that the province's Protestant Unionists, who want to stay British, should be as happy with a political settlement as the 40 percent Catholic minority.
Critics, including Fianna Fail, have dubbed him "Unionist John" and tacitly accused him of betraying his Irish cousins.
On Wednesday night he answered them by saying that he viewed Northern Ireland's Protestants as Irish people as entitled to have their aspirations met as Irish Catholics.

Born on May 18, 1947, the son of a wealthy County Meath farmer, he was educated in Dublin. His economics lecturer at University College was former Fine Gael leader and prime minister Garrett Fitzgerald.
